sn42.12:1.1: Nothing further is known of this chief. His name means “heaper”, perhaps in reference to the wealth that is heaped up and the suffering that is worn away.
sn42.12:2.1: The Buddha repeats the opening of the First Sermon ([sn56.11]()). The text goes on to illustrate these two extremes and the middle way. The lengthy explanation suggests that Rāsiya was slow of understanding.
sn42.12:3.1: This is the first extreme, sensual indulgence. A similar analysis is at [an10.91]().
sn42.12:16.1: This is the second extreme, self mortification.
sn42.12:16.4: In Buddhism, a “skillful quality” would refer to the “ten ways of doing skillful deeds”, which are good qualities for a human life lived well. Beyond that are the “superhuman” states realized by advanced meditators, namely absorptions, psychic powers, and stages of awakening ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj4:4.1.3.1]()).
sn42.12:22.1: The middle way is described as a “wearing away” (_nijjara_). The Jains believed that through the practice of austerities one could “wear away” past bad deeds ([mn14:17.5]()) and future suffering ([mn14:17.8]()). The Buddha distinguishes the term from self-mortification and adapts it for Buddhist use, with “wearing away” applied to the defilements that produce suffering. It is applied to the tenfold path at [an10.106]().
